summary: A day spent in one place is one stay again, not a row every half hour. Everything derived from where people have been — how long they were somewhere, when they usually arrive, what counts as unusual — was being measured against the rate the phone reports its position rather than against what anyone actually did.
details: A stay stays open until something says it ended: the subject moves far enough away, or their position stops being reported for long enough that nothing more can be said. The second of those two clocks was set to 15 minutes. Measured against the live corpus on 2026-09-17 — 26,047 gaps between consecutive positions over 14 days — the 90th-percentile gap is 30.1 minutes and the 99th is 30.2. Fifteen minutes of silence is what somebody sitting still looks like BETWEEN two reports of one stay, not evidence that the stay is over.

Two reports are enough to clear the ten-minute bar for calling something a stay, so the gate fired between every pair: the stay was closed at two reports, the next report started a fresh one, and so on for as long as the person stayed put. The stored history held 3,130 stays where re-deriving the same position reports at the same settings gives 1,399 — a median stay of 30.1 minutes against a re-derived 65.2, with 42% of rows sitting in a 29-32.5 minute band that is the reporting cadence and nothing else.

Both branches now read one clock, 31.7 minutes, which sits above the measured 99th-percentile gap with about a minute and a half of headroom. A stay closes on the clock only for the 0.265% of gaps that are genuinely unusual; every ordinary one keeps the stay open until the subject is observed somewhere else.

The reasoning was already written down. When this hold was last widened, its own comment said the 15-minute clock 'is too short for this job' and gave the resting cadence as the reason — but only the hold was moved onto the wider clock, and the gate that closes the stay was left on the old one, so it fired first and the hold could never be reached. The two are now the same clock, read in both places.

The existing test for this shape fed a whole day in at once and passed, because the batch path was never broken. The new test feeds the reports in one at a time and ticks between them, which is how the service actually runs; before the fix it produced nine two-report stays of thirty minutes each, matching the stored history exactly.
limitations: The stored history is not corrected by this change. Every stay already written keeps its fabricated duration until the derived tables are rebuilt from the underlying position reports, and the typical-arrival and unusual-duration figures derived from them stay wrong until that rebuild lands.

The unusual-duration signal was the worst affected and is still only a counter, never anything said out loud. Its baselines were a median of about 30 minutes with a spread of half a second to five seconds, so a deviation of roughly four seconds was enough to register — it was reporting which stays missed the cadence, not which were unusual. It needs re-measuring once the rebuilt history exists; nothing downstream reads it yet.

The clock is sized against one provider's resting cadence as measured over fourteen days. A provider or a device that reports less often than every 31.7 minutes will still have a single presence split at each longer gap, and nothing detects that automatically — the sizing has to be re-measured if the source changes.

Position reports that stop for longer than the clock still end the stay, which is correct when the phone is off but indistinguishable from it when the phone merely goes quiet somewhere with no signal.
